Powered by id's Quake 3 technology and released in 2001, Gray Matter's Return to Castle Wolfenstein features a tremendous campaign spanning over 25 levels across numerous missions.  Soaking rich in atmosphere and modded to support current widescreen resolutions, the campaign is an excellent precursor to 2014's Wolfenstein A New Order.   

Despite it's age the game plays perfectly.  Combat at times is brutal and difficult.  The AI is a great challenge and surpasses many a modern title.  Weapons are inventive and feature what be may be the most well implemented chain gun ever to grace a video game.   The game falls far short of New Order's stealth mechanics but the combat is so over the top satisfying that I doubt anyone would notice.

Gray Matter Interactive developed Return to Castle Wolfenstein.  The studio was acquired by Activision in 2002 and later merged into Treyarch of Call of Duty fame.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein; a true classic, a phenomenal FPS that has aged well and plays well on modern systems.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is basically THE “I borrowed this game from a friend.” Game. 

You once again play as William “B.J.” Blazkowicz, sent in to stop those cuhraaaazy Nazis from messing with the occult and probably summoning the dead or something. 

RTCW is another game I had a lot of experience with back in the day, especially the multiplayer. The single player starts out in the same vein as Wolfenstein 3D, with Blazkowicz escaping a prison cell before torture with nothing but a Luger and a knife. 

Return to Castle Sniffenscratch runs on the Id Tech 3 engine, the same one they used for Quake III: Arena and Star Trek Voyager: Elite Force. It still looks good, especially for the time, and you get a bunch of neat little effects like shading and dynamic shadows.

Oh baby those 2002 dynamic shadows. 

You have an assortment of weapons to play with, ranging anywhere from standard WW2 pistols and sub-machine guns, to more wacky Nazi super science like a chain gun that blows people up and a testla gun. There isn't much for crunch when shooting at enemies, however, unless you get a chance to blow them up. You do, however, kill most things with a well place head shot, so you can at least start pulling off some rootin' tootin' trick shootin' if you got the aim for it. 

One of the big draws to Return to Castle Chocula was the multiplayer. Which is funnily, deader than Hitler. But back in the day it was pretty poppin'. You played as either Allies or Axis and had a set number of objectives to complete, ranging from escorting an important item or destroying a defensive structure. The Allies would attack and the Axis would defend. It was also surprisingly enough a class based multiplayer instead of the usual arena deathmatch style like Quake III or Unreal Tournament. 

It actually reminds me of Conker's Bad Fur Day's multiplayer, or at least the Tediz vs Squirrel High Command mode. I'm pretty sure Return to Castle Dog Mug inspired the multiplayer for Conker's Live and Reloaded, but I have no way to actually confirm that. Mostly because lead designer: Chris Saevor won't return my calls or answer his door. 

There are more ways to play Return to Castle Huff'n'Puff than this version however. There is also an Xbox port that was ludicrously popular when it first came out, it also came with an extra chapter where B.J. went to Egypt. There was also a PS2 port but I don't care. 

If you're like me, and hurting to play the multiplayer, however, then you're looking in the wrong place. Most people who played Return to Castle Nintendo moved on to Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory, a free multiplayer only spin off to RTCW.  It's still kind of sort of active, so you can at least get a half decent game going to quench that mighty need and go back to playing puzzle pirates or whatever it is you do on your free time. 

Go play RTCW, you'll probably like it. Or don't, I'm not your dad.  It's aged well, or at least to me, but I haven't really left 2003 mentally, so you shouldn't listen to me on the subject.

I'll get straight to the point and say that if you are a fan of older First-person shooters, Return to Castle Wolfenstein is  definitely a worthy purchase. Considering the fact that the game is 16-years-old, it is quite impressive to see how well this title has aged. Being priced at $5, there really is not much reason to not purchase this gem. Hell, you could even wait for a Steam sale and snatch it for even less. 

Pros:

+RTCW has an enjoyably unique storyline set in WWII, but... (See first con below) 
+Environments are relatively varied and levels are usually large enough for multiple approaches to combat
+Enemy variety is solid (You are not only fighting Nazi soldiers, but also the undead, mutated experiments, and more)
+Each section of every mission is a perfect length. None are too long or too short 
+Every weapon feels powerful and useful
+The game manages to be unnervingly creepy, but also humorous with it's drunk Nazis and exaggerated German accents 
+Awesome level of violence 
+Visuals are great for the time 
+Not the longest game out there, but still longer then the average FPS 
+(Mostly) Provides a fair challenge
+The base price is already a steal!

Cons: 

-...Many of the cutscenes progress the story in a mundane way. For instance, when you complete a mission in the game, most of the time the story is progressed with just some of your commanders talking to each other about what you just accomplished. Since these conversations were used as a vehicle to progress the story, the overall narrative became less intriguing to me 
-More or less every boss requires the same strategy to defeat 
-If you go back to a quick-save during combat, it seems that the enemy A.I. get a tactical headstart and are therefore able to pinpoint you quicker then usual. In other words, deaths can feel cheap at times especially when you are low on health 
-Besides the useful secret health and ammunition you find, you can sometimes find treasures and gold which have virtually no use in the game. I would not be surprised if the developers added these in just for the sake of giving the game some more replay value for completionists 
-Repetitive soundtrack that is fitting, but honestly forgettable 
-No widescreen setting since it is old. However, there are mods for that

Overall: 

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is an immensely enjoyable FPS that has aged quite well. Do recommend.

When I was young, me and my family would visit my aunt and uncle a few hours south of us. When we were there, my cousin would sometimes let us raid his box of jewel case PC games. I played many of them (mostly star wars games), but he wouldn't let me play one. Return to Castle Wolfenstein. To get my fix, I would read the manual cover to cover. I was enthraled by its promises of guns, hidden treasures, mutant freaks, and an army of nazis to shoot. I often thought about it for years afterwards, but I never really thought I would play it.

I finaly picked it up here, and I can say, it was worth the wait.

Do you like classic WW2 shooters? The Quake3 engine? Winding castle coridors? Ancient catacombs? Occult spirits and magics? Horifying nazi mutants? If yes to any or all, then this is the game for you.

WARNING: SPOILERS

[b] NOTE: IOrtcw is an absolute requirement for modern PCs - it's a fan made patch that is essential - you CANNOT play without it on Windows 10! [/b]

An absolutely fantastic first person shooter. 

I'll cover the game's [b] gameplay, storyline, graphics, sound and multiplayer, as well as performance. [/b]

Gameplay wise, the game is absolutely flawless. It's a hard game, with Nazi soldiers and twisted occult monsters draining your health pretty quickly if you don't finish them off first. Most enemies, if not all enemies, have their own unique idiosyncracies and features to switch up the gameplay. 

Nazi soldiers, for instance, will sound nearby alarms if the player is spotted. Fallschirmjager paratroopers use more powerful weapons and have good body armour, but don't wear helmets. Zombies have a ranged spirit attack and a close range swipe attack, and can also get up once after being killed unless you destroy their bones to powder. These are just a few examples, and there are actually quite a few realistic enemy types.

The weapons in the game are absolutely sublime. You start out with poor weapons, like the Luger pistol, and slowly progress to Nazi-made MP40 SMGs, US Thompson sub machine guns, and even some exotic weapons like the FG42, a slow-firing but powerful battle rifle with a scope. You also get to use some awesome fictional weaponry, like the Snooper rifle, a silenced rifle with a built-in night vision function, and the Venom, a ridiculously powerful man-portable minigun. Awesome.

Storyline wise, I am not going to spoil things but it's a very cool storyline, packed with backstairs intrigue and espionage... and the Occult.

Graphically the game isn't great, as can be expected from such an old game. However, it's not bad; the good art style makes the graphics bearable, and it only really requires a fan-made HD texture pack to make it look pretty good. Player animations are slightly jerky, but the character animations are excellent... other than the lip sync. The environments are also absolutely class, they look amazing and are immersive - not what you'd expect from such an old game. You practically feel the cold on your skin in Norway, or the heat of the sun in the forest areas. It's impressive, to say the least.

The sound design of the game is absolutely superb, I cannot recommend a good pair of headphones or speakers highly enough to experience this game. The guns sound powerful and have a frankly impressive degree of punch, all sounds realistically fade out when you're further away, and the voice acting is more than acceptable... in fact, the voice actor for General Deathshead is brilliant, his delivery during the X-labs showdown is absolutely chilling...

The music is a similar story. It is an orchestral masterpiece, ranging from relatively straightforward orchestral pieces to chilling ambience which is reminiscent of Mutato Muzika's work on Crash Bandicoot in it's impressive use of mechanical samples to act as intruments - you'll see what I mean if you check out the X-labs soundtrack. From the subtle creepy ambience of the slower areas of the game, to the explosive, bombastic action music, it fits the tone and blend seamlessly with the environment.

The multiplayer is excellent too, if not slightly dead. It's very TF2-esque in it's delivery, it's class based and each class obviously has it's benefits and drawbacks. It later spawned Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory, which built upon the RTCW multiplayer superbly - it's free, too, and I would recommend that over RTCW if you're looking for MP, as it plays the same (perhaps better), is more stable, and has a big playerbase to this day. 

Performance is excellent, you'll stay glued to your monitor's refresh rate if you need to. From crap laptops (I'm talking 2002 laptops!) to modern PCs you'll do very well, it's impressive. There are so many options to tweak too. That being said - and you must take this advice  - it WILL NOT WORK on Windows 10 without ioRTCW. No iffs, no buts. ioRTCW adds so many new features, it totally saves the game. 

In conclusion, this game is a true 9/10. I know this review doesn't cover many negatives, but that's simply because there aren't many!

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a classic. I grew up playing this game and I highly recommended it if you're into old-school/boomer shooters. The devs incorporated and mashed several different genres and themes to create a very unique experience. Some levels feature pure action while others include elements of horror as well as sci-fi. There are also a couple of stealth sections. Every level has a different look and feel to it and you won't find yourself in the same environment twice and that's saying something. There are tons of enemy variety throughout the campaign and lots of different guns at your disposal. 

The story is just okay imo and sometimes it can feel a bit corny, like a bad Hollywood movie, but that's part of it's charm. The voice acting is nothing special and the cutscenes were alright and fits the theme and tone of the game. Some of the bosses look ridiculous. The game runs on some old Quake engine and the graphics have aged considerably. Environments look a little rough especially the outdoor scenery but it's expected given it's age. I just wished if the devs had tone-downed supernatural elements a bit. Combat is generally awesome with a few minor hiccups from time to time and bugs. The game also crashed 3 times on my roughly 8 hour playthrough (might have something to do with Windows 10 but not sure). As for the music there aren't any songs or a cool theme song but I guess it's alright if you're just going to have some fun. 

RTCW is still an old-school game at heart and so yes, it can be quite difficult during the later stages of the game. Many of the mini bosses with flamethrowers and mini-gun will instantly crush you to death. Even regular soldiers and Nazi zombies get pinpoint accuracy in killing you and headshots also get less accurate for some reason as you progress further. Make sure to quick save often! 

Overall RTCW is still great today and doesn't overstay it's welcome during it's 6-8 hour campaign. It's not for everyone, if you're expecting it to play like a modern FPS like Wolfenstein 2014 or Doom 2016 reboot then you're going to be left disappointed. It also requires community fixes and patches to run properly on modern hardware with 19:6 widescreen support at high resolution.

Hope to see a fan-made remake of this game in RTX Remix with path-tracing features!

Return To Castle Wolfenstein is a first-person shooter reboot of the Wolfenstein series which much like its predecessor focuses on fast-paced gunplay with a number of improvements made to compensate for the new engine technologies available at the time. 

Firstly, unlike Wolfenstein 3D, the developers actually tried to implement a compelling story to a franchise known for not actually having a “story”. To some degree, the story in this game, at least from a concept point of view, brings something new to the table by adding elements of occult. The plot revolves around the American soldier, B.J. Blazkowicz, trying to impede the Nazis from discovering and extracting a serum hidden in an ancient tomb capable of augmenting soldiers into “Dark Knights”, an evil undead army from the 9th Century. Nazis and occult? Absurd bollocks, but what’s not to like. However, while the concept does enhance the single-player campaign, the story itself is mostly ignorable since it generally feels like it is there to fill in the space. Blazkowicz, while a total badass, still remains one of the blandest protagonists in existence. He takes orders from his superiors like a puppet with no remorse or personal motives. Even when the Allies want to give him a medal for his efforts and persumably a well deserved break at the end, he is somewhere outside still kicking Nazi butt. Boy, he sure is souless; born with only one scope in life: to kill Nazis for eternity. Plus, it is silly how the Allies' solution to most problems is to send a "one-man army" to take down Nazi headquarters single-handedly without even breaking a sweat. But that is Wolfenstein after all; it purposely does not need to explain how Blazkowicz does it -- and hey, some ancient voodoo magic is involved, so anything is justifiable, right? Fortunately, the story did manage to create the cool villain by the name of Deathshead, who later becomes the franchise’s main antagonist.

The gunplay in here is hasty but satisfying, reminiscent of older games such as Quake, Doom and Unreal Tournament, and unquestionably the strongest point of the game. While it all boils down to sprinting and shooting enemies in quick manners, the game does offer some moments of straightforward stealth where you get to sneak behind enemy lines. Additionally, there is an adequate variety in enemies from the deadly female squads in tight leather uniforms (those butts though) to juggernauts like the Über-Soldats. Different weapons are at Blazkowicz’s disposal too, with the Tesla gun being the most fun one to use, even if the MP40 probably becomes the most practical throughout most of the game, thus making pistols pretty redundant. One problem with the weapons though is the fact you never seem to run out of ammo. Retrospectively now, the gunplay does feel very basic, but mostly thanks to its fast paced action killing waves of enemies does not get dull, surprisingly enough.

The level design has the mentality of most shooters back in the late '90s and early noughties based on maze-like corridors and paths, essentially allowing the player the freedom to pick whichever route to travel back and forth within the somewhat confined space. Exploration is also encouraged and rewarded by finding secret chambers filled with collectables, even if these give no gameplay advantages to the player. Graphically, at the time, the game looked great but as time went by its visuals sure look dated today. On the other hand, the same cannot be said to its soundtrack which even to this day remains memorable and rather ageless. When you can recognise a level/map by a specific track from the soundtrack, then you know the soundtrack left a good impression.

Boasting a strong single-player campaign, (wherther you take the story seriously or not), many probably remember the game for its multiplayer component which at the time was very popular and considered by many superior than the campaign, even as far as being regarded one of the best multiplayer components in a game ever. I cannnot argue with that, although it was not until the highly acclaimed free standalone Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory came out that the multiplayer component peaked in popularity. Featuring a class-based gameplay similar to Team Fortress, two teams (Allies and Axis) fight each other to complete objectives on various maps. Personally, I spent far too many hours in the multiplayer alone when I was younger because it was balanced and had a very enjoyable experience. Currently, the multiplayer from Return To Castle Wolfenstein seems dead. Rest in peace.

In conclusion, Return To Castle Wolfenstein still remains a classic in the eyes of many, including myself, who played it in its heydays online and/or offline, and a milestone on PC. But it definitely lost its relevance and appeal to the general public as years have passed due to more ambitious and realistic shooters showing up years later. More old-school than modern, it still is a solid shooter, nevertheless, which does not spoil the player with today’s regenerative health and cover-base mechanics and can still provide enough hours of fun mindlessly killing Nazis. Pick it up only for nostalgic purposes or if you are curious to see how fast-paced shooters were like more than a decade ago in case you never grew up with them.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a definitive masterpiece from the golden age of PC gaming that still holds its ground as a uniquely atmospheric shooter. For many players, it was a foundational experience, a game that successfully modernised the "run and gun" mechanics of its predecessor while introducing a dark, supernatural edge that redefined what a World War II shooter could be.

The game’s greatest strength is its tonal variety. While it begins as a traditional escape-from-prison military shooter, it quickly descends into genuine horror. The legendary catacombs levels, filled with armored undead and terrifying, lightning-emitting "lopers," served as peak horror for many players of that era. The sound design, eerie rattles in the dark and the sudden hiss of supernatural foes remains deeply unsettling, proving that you don't need modern graphics to create a sense of absolute dread.

Playing as Agent B.J. Blazkowicz, you truly feel like a one-man army pitted against the mythical pursuits of the SS Paranormal Division. The story is charmingly cheesy, leaning into its Indiana Jones meets sci-fi aesthetic with a lovable sincerity. Whether you’re sabotaging V2 rockets or fighting the resurrected Heinrich I, the game provides a constant sense of progression and scale. The arsenal is equally impressive, blending historically accurate WWII weaponry with experimental prototypes like the Tesla Gun and Venom Gatling gun, ensuring there is always a fresh way to dispatch your foes.

Despite its age, the game’s core mechanics, fluid movement and challenging AI that uses cover and retreats remain surprisingly robust. While it features sudden difficulty spikes and dated stealth missions, these flaws are often seen as part of its old-school charm.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is more than just a nostalgia trip. It is a perfectly balanced blend of action, horror, and sci-fi that most modern shooters struggle to emulate. If you were there to experience it at the time, playing it now is a powerful reminder of why we fell in love with FPS games in the first place.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a landmark first-person shooter that represents a crucial moment in the evolution of the genre, blending classic run-and-gun design with horror elements and cinematic ambition in a way that felt bold at the time and still feels distinctive today. Set during World War II but infused with occult experimentation and pulp-style sci-fi, the game places players once again in the boots of B.J. Blazkowicz as he infiltrates Nazi strongholds, secret research facilities, and supernatural horrors lurking beneath the surface of the war. This hybrid premise gives the game a unique identity, balancing historical grit with fantastical escalation that steadily grows more intense as the campaign unfolds.

The single-player campaign is one of the game’s strongest aspects, offering a lengthy and varied journey that moves confidently between stealth-leaning infiltration, explosive firefights, and eerie horror-themed sequences. Early missions emphasize sneaking, silenced weapons, and careful positioning, gradually giving way to more aggressive encounters once the player’s arsenal expands. The pacing feels deliberate, with levels designed to encourage exploration, hidden secrets, and tactical engagement rather than constant forward momentum. Enemy placement and encounter design demand awareness and patience, and the game is not afraid to punish reckless play, especially on higher difficulty settings. This creates a sense of tension and accomplishment that rewards methodical progress rather than reflexive shooting alone.

Combat itself reflects an era before modern shooter conventions fully took hold, relying on health packs, armor pickups, and manually managed resources instead of regenerating health or streamlined systems. Weapons feel weighty and purposeful, from conventional firearms to experimental and supernatural tools that reinforce the game’s shifting tone. While the gunplay may feel less fluid or forgiving to players accustomed to contemporary shooters, it retains a satisfying rhythm rooted in precision, positioning, and situational awareness. Enemy AI, though dated by modern standards, still offers credible resistance, especially when enemies coordinate or attack from multiple angles.

Atmosphere is where Return to Castle Wolfenstein truly excels. The level design, lighting, and environmental storytelling work together to create spaces that feel oppressive, hostile, and steeped in mystery. Gothic architecture, underground crypts, snowbound fortresses, and industrial laboratories each contribute to a sense of place that remains memorable long after individual encounters fade. The gradual introduction of supernatural elements is particularly effective, transforming what begins as a relatively grounded war shooter into something far more unsettling. Sound design and music reinforce this mood, using ambient cues, distant noises, and dramatic scoring to heighten suspense and underline key moments.

Beyond its single-player campaign, the game’s legacy is strongly tied to its multiplayer component, which laid the groundwork for class-based, objective-focused shooters. The multiplayer design emphasized teamwork, defined roles, and coordinated objectives rather than simple deathmatch scoring, influencing later titles and eventually evolving into the standalone Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory. Even though the original multiplayer may feel dated today, its design philosophy remains influential, and its impact on competitive and cooperative shooter design is difficult to overstate.

Looking back, Return to Castle Wolfenstein stands as both a product of its time and a foundation for what came after. Some elements undeniably show their age, from movement and animation to interface design, but these rough edges are balanced by strong fundamentals, confident atmosphere, and a clear creative vision. It remains a compelling experience for players who appreciate classic shooters, deliberate pacing, and a willingness to blend genres without restraint. Rather than feeling obsolete, it feels like a snapshot of a moment when shooters were experimenting boldly, and that sense of identity continues to give the game lasting relevance.

It had been a long time coming for the 2001 release of Return to Castle Wolfenstein. The last main title in the franchise to be released was Wolfenstein 3D: Spear of Destiny in 1992, which saw the subsequent release of two mission packs, Return to Danger and Ultimate Challenge, in 1994. Needless to say, fans of the series were sure that it was dead, left to be a relic of the past, albeit an important one that birthed first-person shooters. However, when the genre expanded into the realm of more advanced 3D graphics, id Software seized the moment to resurrect Wolfenstein from the brink of extinction.

Putting its first spin on a richly detailed story arc, the introductory cutscene of Return to Castle Wolfenstein dates back to 943 AD where Heinrich, a German prince who dominated Western Europe with his army of the undead, is stopped by a monk who seals him in an underground tomb. Fast-forward to a thousand years later in 1943, Heinrich Himmler, the Chief of the Nazi SS, is researching any possible way to win World War II through a combination of science and black magic. In doing so, Himmler comes across stories of Heinrich, and becomes deeply interested in bringing the German prince back to life, and as such the SS Paranormal Division is born. Our fated hero, B.J. Blazkowicz, and his partner known only as Agent One, had been captured by Nazi forces and taken to Castle Wolfenstein to be tortured for information. Blazkowicz survives, his partner does not, and he must escape the Nazi compound and stop Himmler, Deathshead, and their abominations.

If you've played any shooter from the early 2000's, then you'll already know what to mostly expect from this title. However, the action is incredibly fast-paced, a trait that has stayed a series staple even through the most recent installments. That being said, there are missions that require stealth, as setting off an alarm will result in a game over, which is a series first for Wolfenstein. In fact, being stealthy in missions that do not require such acts is beneficial to the player, since the damage that is taken by any bullet whatsoever is ridiculously high, which in turn makes the gameplay difficult even on the easiest setting. 

There is a ton of diversity over the course of 7 chapters, which are separated into 26 missions. From snowy tundras, to open compounds, narrow villages with multiple buildings to explore, creepy catacombs, vast castles, and even a graveyard. The atmosphere is thick, with many levels being laden with cobwebs, mist, fog, and even lightning; not to mention, explosions galore. There are also a good amount of enemies to face off against, ranging from the standard Nazi SS and paratroopers to skeletons, mummies, and deadly mutant abominations. Likewise, there's no shortage of weaponry to use to take down these foes; flamethrowers, Panzerfausts, Stens, MP 40s, Colts, Lugars, and more await use, including the electricity-using Tesla and a Nazi-invented machine gun known as Venom.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is the first chance that the series had to really dig its heels in and tell a worth-while story, which it does really well through various cutscenes and written briefings that appear before each mission. There are also many odes and nods to Wolfenstein 3D and its predecessor, Spear of Destiny, and even Blazkowicz's escape from Castle Wolfenstein is a mirroring of the first and second episodes of Wolfenstein 3D. The atmosphere of the game is worth lumping into a horror-inspired category, as many of the levels deal with resurrected skeletons, mummies, supernatural entities, and sci-fi mutants. Even if you are someone who didn't enjoy playing the two retro FPS titles in the franchise, Return to Castle Wolfenstein may very well distill your taste for the series, as it's one of the very best early-modern FPS games to date.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is one of the classic Wolfenstein games, made on the Quake engine in the early 2000s. While a lot of people insist this is one of the best Wolfenstein games ever made, an essential FPS of the early era, and still holds up today, I disagree. RTCW has its high points, but also abysmally low ones as well.

(This review was based on a single playthrough, on what was basically medium difficulty out of three options.)

Let's start with the positives. 

[h1]Positives[/h1]

[b]Immersive Atmosphere[/b]
The atmosphere and level design are amazing. Having any sort of weather effect adds a lot to a game, and RTCW wasn't afraid to get a little foggy or snowy. This obscures your sight, just like real weather would. It also has complex but logical lab layouts, making them feel like it could be a real place. RTCW builds a world that seems just as possible as the WW2 we learn about in 8th grade history.

[b]Cliche but Enjoyable Story[/b]
The story is also worthy of some praise, despite its slight cheesiness. It's just what you would expect out of a Wolfenstein game: Germany is researching the occult and enhancing its soldiers with robotics. Eventually they get mechanized soldiers and you have to fight them. It's formulaic, but effective. It gets the point across and while the German soldiers do have comically fake accents, they and the Allied Forces generals are well acted and are pleasant to listen to.

Unfortunately, the positives of Return to Castle Wolfenstein cannot outweight the negatives. While the first half of the game does not suffer from these problems, the ending levels are plagued with them.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]

[b]God-Awful Enemies[/b]
The enemies are offensively bad in design. There is almost a sort of aimbot switch going on, where a single soldier can miss an entire magazine of shots but then land 20 of them in a row flawlessly (Even if you are strafing or peppering them with your own bullets), depleting over half your health and armor. Enemy snipers can also have the same problem, able to land shots at such a great distance that you can barely even see them, let alone snipe them back before half your health is gone. This "boosted" response time and accuracy is courtesy of the difficulty system, which isn't increasing the difficulty at all, just the omnipotence of the enemies. Notice how I do not say this game is HARD. It is just bad AI that leeches the enjoyment out of the game. While this is insultingly bad AI, it is tolerable through the use of cover and smart positioning. This goes out the window in the final three levels.

[b]F*ck Lopers and Super Soldiers[/b]
The final levels introduce Lopers and Super Soldiers. Lopers are incredibly fast moving enemies that can either attack by using a massive electric AOE attack, or by jumping at you at an incredible distance. This jump is fast, nearly unavoidable, and does huge damage in a massive area despite no attack being visible. I was killed by a Loper 5 meters below me while on a catwalk above just because he was jumping around on the ground floor, but somehow still hitting me. Super Soldiers are even more offensively bad, as the prototype soldiers are quite content to spam endless rounds of either RPG rockets or minigun bullets in your direction with no pause. The complete Super Soldiers also use a Tesla Cannon, which is an electric beam (With infinite ammunition, of course) that will not miss, has nearly unlimited range, pushes the player back and deals staggeringly high amounts of damage with absolutely no drawbacks. All encounters with the Tesla Super Soldiers take place in rooms with nearly no cover or way to avoid their fire. This is horrible, unfair and unfun enemy design, and whoever thought these enemies were acceptable for public release need to reconsider their career choices.

[b]Mandatory Save Scumming[/b]
The biggest problem with this game is the massive difficulty spike the player faces if they are not constantly quick saving. I do not look down on save-scumming, but when it is close to the only viable way to complete a game there is something seriously wrong with said game. The Quake engine is not designed for stealth, many enemies have near endless sightlines and can see you and shoot you well before you even know which direction they are in. And of course when they see you, the entire enemy compound somehow knows which exact rock you are hiding behind and go on full alert. This near instant change in the situation makes quick saving after every twenty feet or bit of progress the only way to not ruin an entire mission just because an enemy partially obscured behind a bush two miles away saw you peek out from behind a wall, or turning a corner and instantly losing 50 health & 80 armor to a single man with a Panzerfaust. Return to Castle Wolfenstein is more of a trial and error game than a proper skill and positioning FPS.

[b]Insultingly Bad Bosses[/b]
The pinnacle of dissapointment lies in the bosses of the game. The first and final boss are hilariously easy, as they can only use melee and limited, easily dodged ranged attacks. The easiest and most effective way to beat them is to simply stand 10 meters away and pepper the walking sponges with bullets until they eventually explode. The final boss is even more of a dissapointment than the first, because after a whole 2 levels solely dedicated to padding the game length before the boss you get to face a heavily armored man that can ONLY use melee, and occasionally summons normal zombies to join the fight. The second boss of the game is more offensive than the other two simply for being one of the aformentioned Tesla Super Soldiers. The instant the fight starts, 8 out of 10 times he locks onto you with the Tesla gun and wipes out a solid chunk of your health before you can even attempt to find what little cover there is in the boss arena. It is a gimmicky dissapointment. 

[b]A lot of the fans of RTCW are nostalgia blinded maniacs[/b]
I specifically leave this here, not because of the game itself but because no matter where you go, any criticism of Return to Castle Wolfenstein is swiftly met with unending hate troll spam. Any forum you go on that talks bad about this game is met with thunderous dissaproval, let alone just this review. If steam hadn't removed the percentage approved feature on review ratings, you would see how many downvotes this review got. Not because its a bad review, but because the nostalgia blinded fans cannot imagine for a second that their precious baby is flawed in any way. You have no idea how many comments I deleted because they brought absolutely nothing to the table except troll bait attempts. If you want help in beating this crappy game, be warned. The community here is more likely to tell you to Git Gud than a Dark Souls player. No matter how good you are at games, they will INSIST you are bad and "can't handle a game that doesn't hold your hand". Not that you should get this game in the first place.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
In summary, Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a gimmicky, broken piece of crap that happens to have a fantastic atmosphere and surprisingly good visuals for a game made in 2001. No amount of personal skill can help you overcome the bad AI and unbalanced weapons (I've been playing games for nearly 20 years now, you could not pay me to believe I have not "gotten good", especially when I've done Halo 2 on Legendary) Do not believe the nostalgia blinded fans, many of which will downvote this review and prove my point (Even though the ratings are supposed to be "Is this review helpful?" not "Do you agree with this review?") No matter what the price is, this game is not worth your money. Go buy Half Life, which came out 3 years earlier and is somehow better in every aspect, and still costs about the same as this game.

Explanation and reason you want to lock your FPS to lower than 60fps - 

Today we have gaming PC's running at least 10x (4Ghz and Greater) that on top of the amount of running anywhere from 4-16 cores in the CPU and playing at frame rates greater than 60 fps. This turns many of the more difficult enemies into essentially aimbots; like Snipers are a lot more deadly being able to track, aim quicker and fire more accurately. This also makes the Flamethrower Soldier, Fire Zombie, Loper, Occult Priest, Proto-soldier variants, Venom Gunner extremely dangerous and difficult to fight because the damage happens faster. Especially the Loper's where their Electric attack damage actually causing damage faster taking huge chunks of your health even in the easy difficulty mode. 

-----

With all that being said. The graphics still hold up and at higher resolutions like 1440p and 4K, its astounding how well many textures are detailed and actually in a super high resolution from back then without using any HD Texture Packs.

Audio is great and the sound track great. 

Story is well fitting for the [d] universe.

I havent tried the Enemy Territory multiplayer since the servers were brought back but i remember that portion being real fun back in the day.

I still give this game a [b]8.5/10[/b] despite some of the nuances from modern PC's affecting the gameplay.
